sweep_summary: bora1271 (Borana-Arsi-Guji Oromo) is not in the catalog. Of the four works with stress in the title, one is noise (Foot 1913/1968 dictionary — the keyword is the surname; HathiTrust has a full-view copy but blocks our network), two are the same article (Gamta 1999, Glottolog duplicate records), and one is unreachable (Moreno 1935/37 RSO 16, 38 pp. on Galla accent; only a second-hand line from his 1939 grammar via Appleyard: accent 'molto instabile'). Gamta 1999 was downloaded from the Oromo Studies Association's open back-issue archive and read: native-speaker word-stress rules for the author's idiolect — penultimate stress before final short -a, final stress otherwise, minimal pairs by stress+syllabification; dialect unnamed, tonal-accent literature ignored. The Borana-specific accent descriptions (Owens 1980 African Language Studies 17; Stroomer 1987/1995; Andrzejewski 1957 BSOAS, DOI 10.1017/S0041977X00133117) remain print/paywalled; Appleyard 1991 (held by the project) summarises Owens: masculine disyllables ultimate accent, feminine penultimate, in a high/low tonal-accent system.

new_statements.quote: Harar Oromo, like Booran, has a tone system which consists of three main parts: a classification of roots and affixes in terms of basic tone; a specification of the contexts where these basic tones may/must occur; and rules altering the tone on certain morphemes in certain contexts. [...] sketched in its basic outline by Andrzejewski (1957, 1966). I should note that I have found no lexical minimal pairs distinguished by tone alone in Harar Oromo. [...] First of all, only the penultimate or final syllable of a root can have a high tone, and all nominals except a few pronouns, demonstratives, and numerals (2.1.1) have at least one high tone. new_statements.rule_in_words: Oromo (Harar, and by the author's explicit first-hand comparison, Booran) is a tonal-accent language, not a stress language: each nominal carries a lexically/morphologically given 'basic' high tone confined to a two-syllable window at the right edge of the root — H on the final syllable, or on penult+final (a penult H entails a final H); which of the two is only partly predictable from stem shape (CVCa → LH; -aa-final mostly penult-low; long non-low final vowel mostly penult-high) and, in Booran per Owens 1980 as reported by Appleyard 1991, from gender (disyllabic masculines final H, feminines penult H). Verbs are inherently toneless and get fixed H from particular TAM morphology (jussive H on first syllable; negative imperative H on penult). Long-vowel suffixes place H on the preceding syllable; adding suffixes moves H rightward so it never sits on an antepenult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described by Owens (single H span per nominal; no secondary prominence). Hodson & Walker 1922 mention 'secondary accent' in long words but leave it unmarked.
new_statements.exceptions: A few pronouns, demonstratives, possessives and numerals are all-low (no H); invariable adjectives ending in a long vowel mostly have low penult (adii, guutuu) against the long-vowel tendency; four long-vowel suffixes (-aa verbal noun, -aa participial, -uu concurrent, nominative) fail to induce H; loans not treated separately.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level 'basic tone' is defined in a citation-like frame (noun as object of an imperative); in other syntactic contexts (e.g. before demonstratives, in non-'fixed-tone' clauses) a nominal may surface all-low or with predicate-nominal tone, so surface pitch is phrase/syntax-conditioned. The positional rule is stated for Harar Oromo; its extension to Booran rests on Owens's sentence 'like Booran' plus his 1980 Booran study (not accessible), summarized second-hand by Appleyard 1991 and Mous 2022.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted first-hand statement (Owens 1985) describes Harar/Eastern Oromo (Glottolog east2652, ISO hae), with the author's explicit first-hand assertion that Booran shares the same tone system (Owens had published the Booran tone study in 1980). The Borana-specific locus facts (disyllabic masculine nouns final H, feminines penultimate H; Owens 1980: 149-150) are available only second-hand (Appleyard 1991; Mous 2022). Hodson & Walker 1922 ('tonic accent on the penultimate in the vast majority of cases') is first-hand but describes a composite 'Galla' — Hodson's material from Mega in Borana country, Walker's from Gore in western Oromo (west2721) — and Andrzejewski 1957 explicitly lists it among grammars of dialects that 'differ from Borana in many details'. All modern Borana sources concern the Borana (Boraana/Booran) dialect of Kenya/southern Ethiopia; nothing was found for the Arsi or Guji members of bora1271.

new_statements.quote: In the case of Afaan Oromo, stress should be understood to mean a relative syllable strength that depends on the quality and quantity of the vowel ... the following word stress rules, based on the writer's idiolect, are presented. Rule 1. In a CV.CV/V.CV/VV.CV pattern, where the final V is -a, the stress usually falls on the first syllable ... Rule 4. In a CV.CV/V.CV/VV.CV pattern, where the final V is other than the single vowel -a, the second syllable is stressed ... Rule 7. When a three-syllable structure ends in -a, the stress usually occurs on the penult ... Rule 8. When a word ends in vowels other than -a, the last syllable in a word is usually stressed.
new_statements.citation: Gamta, Tilahun (Xilaahun Gamtaa). 1999. Structural and word stress patterns in Afaan Oromo. Journal of Oromo Studies 6(1-2): 173-194.
new_statements.locator: §3.2 Word Stress Patterns, printed pp. 187-190 (PDF pp. 199-202)
new_statements.reading: Native-speaker, first-hand but self-described provisional rules for one idiolect: stress is penultimate when the word ends in short -a and final when it ends in any other vowel (long vowels attract it); a few disyllables are distinguished by stress plus syllabification. The dialect is not named and may be the Ethiopian standard rather than Borana-Arsi-Guji, and the account ignores the tonal-accent analyses of Owens 1980/1985; it is nonetheless the only dedicated Oromo word-stress study readable in this search of works with stress in the title. Hodson & Walker 1922 (penultimate default, acute for exceptions; partly Borana data) is the only other first-hand statement held by the project.

sources.quote: § 8.—In the vast majority of cases the tonic accent will be found to fall on the penultimate syllable. When a word, then, is not a monosyllable, it may be inferred, in reading or recitation, that this stress, in the absence of any mark to the contrary, is to fall on the last syllable but one. Such words are left unaccented, e.g. meika, ... Where the accent of a word (not being a monosyllable) is oxytone or proparoxytone, or where the accent is further back than the propenultimate, the syllable stressed or accented is marked with a ', e.g. besán, isán, afar, intali, nánbita, sátini, wáraqata.
